interviewQuestions.question: How would you find the first and last occurrence of a target value in a sorted array with duplicates, in O(log n)?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The key adjustment from plain binary search: a match at `arr[mid] == target` is never an immediate final answer — it's a candidate that might be improved by continuing to search in one specific direction.

For the **first** occurrence: when I find a match, I record it as the current best candidate, then keep searching the **left** half (`hi = mid - 1`) to see if an even earlier occurrence exists. For the **last** occurrence, it's the mirror image — record the match, then search the **right** half (`lo = mid + 1`). Both variants still only ever discard half the remaining window per step, so each is O(log n), and I can share one parameterized helper function between them, differing only in which side continues searching after a match.

A clean way to frame this out loud: finding the first occurrence is really just `lower_bound(arr, target)` — the first index where `arr[i] >= target` — and separately confirming that index actually holds the target (since `lower_bound` doesn't require the target to be present at all). I'd mention that connection explicitly, since it shows I see these as instances of the same boundary-search pattern rather than three unrelated tricks.

**Testing:** whether you understand that a match is a candidate to be improved, not a stopping condition, which is the actual insight distinguishing this from plain existence search.

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through searching a rotated sorted array in O(log n), and explain why binary search still applies even though the array isn't fully sorted.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The insight that rescues binary search here: no matter where you split a rotated sorted array at any midpoint, **at least one of the two resulting halves is still properly sorted** — the rotation can only break the order at one single point, so it can affect at most one of the two halves at a time.

So at each step, I first determine which half is sorted by comparing endpoints — `arr[lo] <= arr[mid]` means the left half is sorted; otherwise the right half is. Then I check whether the target falls within that sorted half's value range. If it does, I recurse into that half using ordinary comparison logic, since it behaves exactly like a normal sorted sub-array. If it doesn't, the target — if present at all — must be in the other, not-currently-sorted-looking half, so I recurse there instead, trusting that on the *next* iteration, one of its two sub-halves will again be cleanly sorted.

Every iteration still discards exactly half the remaining window, so the complexity stays O(log n) — the only overhead per step is the extra constant-time comparison to figure out which half is sorted, which doesn't change the asymptotic bound.

A specific bug I'd flag from experience: hard-coding an assumption about which half is always sorted, instead of checking `arr[lo]` vs `arr[mid]` explicitly every iteration — which half is sorted flips depending on where the rotation point currently sits relative to `mid`, and it's a mistake that silently fails on roughly half of all possible rotations while appearing to work on the other half.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the 'one half is always sorted' guarantee precisely, which is the actual proof this technique relies on.

interviewQuestions.question: How does having duplicate values change the complexity of searching a rotated sorted array?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Without duplicates, comparing `arr[lo]` to `arr[mid]` always tells you unambiguously which half is sorted, preserving the clean O(log n) bound. With duplicates, there's a genuinely ambiguous case: if `arr[lo] == arr[mid] == arr[hi]`, that comparison gives you no information at all — both halves could plausibly contain the rotation point, and you can't tell which from this check alone.

The standard fix when that ambiguous case is hit: shrink the window by one element from each side (`lo += 1, hi -= 1`) and retry, rather than confidently halving. This is a real, provable cost, not a theoretical footnote — on an array that's entirely one repeated value (the worst case for this ambiguity), you're forced to shrink one element at a time every single iteration, degrading the worst case to **O(n)**.

I'd present this as a genuine trade-off to discuss with an interviewer rather than something to silently patch around: if duplicates are a real possibility in the input and worst-case guarantees matter, it's worth explicitly noting that the O(log n) bound is conditional on the array not being pathologically full of ties, and that no algorithm can do better in the fully-ambiguous case without additional information (like an explicit rotation count stored separately from the array itself).

**Testing:** whether you know this is a genuine complexity degradation with a specific trigger condition, not just "duplicates make things harder" in the abstract.

interviewQuestions.question: A production API endpoint searches a rotated, cached sorted dataset (rotated because it's a circular buffer of recent events) and is intermittently returning stale or missing results under concurrent writes. How would you approach this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Rotated-array binary search assumes the array is a stable, consistent snapshot for the entire duration of the search — every comparison (`arr[lo]` vs `arr[mid]`, then target against a half's range) implicitly relies on the array not changing mid-search. If the circular buffer is being concurrently written to (new events pushed in, old ones evicted, potentially shifting the rotation point) while a search is in flight, the algorithm can end up comparing against a version of the array that's internally inconsistent across different reads — some reads reflecting the pre-write state, others post-write — which breaks the very invariant (one half is always sorted) the algorithm depends on.

I'd first confirm whether reads during the search are actually snapshot-consistent. If the underlying storage allows a read to see a partially-updated buffer (a write in progress touching some but not all of the elements a single search will read), that's the direct cause, and the fix is ensuring the search operates over an immutable snapshot — e.g., a copy-on-write structure, or a read that acquires a consistent view (a version number or timestamp check) before beginning, rather than reading live mutable state field by field.

Second, I'd check whether the rotation itself is being tracked as metadata (an explicit "head" index) separately from the array's raw layout, or being re-derived by scanning for the break point on every search — if it's re-derived, a concurrent write between "find the rotation point" and "search using it" is its own race condition, distinct from the array-mutation issue above.

The general principle I'd apply: binary search variants are correctness-sensitive to the *entire* search window being stable across all comparisons in a single search — anything that can mutate mid-search, concurrency being the most common real-world cause, needs either a snapshot/copy strategy or a lock, and "intermittent" symptoms specifically (versus consistently wrong) is a strong signal pointing at a race rather than a logic bug.

**Testing:** whether you can extend the algorithm's correctness assumptions (stable input) to a concurrent production system and diagnose a race condition rather than treating this as a pure algorithm bug.
